results.title: Post-stratification and calibration
results.content: Post-stratification, raking, and calibration (or GREG estimation) are related ways of using auxiliary information available on the whole population. These methods all involve adjusting the sampling weights so that the known population totals for auxiliary variables are reproduced exactly. We supply a formula ~stype and must specify population totals for the design matrix produced by this formula. pop.totals<-c(`(Intercept)`=6194, stypeH=755, stypeM=1018) dclus1g<-calibrate(dclus1, ~stype, pop.totals). Calibration to a single factor variable is equivalent to post-stratification, as we see from these examples:. We can calibrate using the two variables stype and sch.wide, as we did with raking above. > dclus1g2 <- calibrate(dclus1, ~stype+sch.wide, c(pop.totals, sch.wideYes=5122)) > svymean(~api00, dclus1g2) mean SE api00 641 23.829 > svytotal(~enroll, dclus1g2) total SE enroll 3654414 403074 > svytotal(~stype, dclus1g2) total SE stypeE 4421 4.704e-14 stypeH 755 2.921e-15 stypeM 1018 3.821e-14. > dstrat <- svydesign(id = ~1, strata = ~stype, weights = ~pw, + data = apistrat, fpc = ~fpc) > ratio <- svyratio(~api.stu, ~enroll, dstrat, separate = FALSE) > predict(ratio, total=3811472) $total enroll api.stu 3190038 $se enroll api.stu 29565.98 > dstratg <- calibrate(dstrat, ~enroll-1, pop=3811472, lambda=1) > svytotal(~api.stu, dstratg) total SE api.stu 3190038 29566. Two refinements of regression calibration are the ability to impose bounds ont he calibration weights and to require that the weights are constant within sampling units. > (dclus1g3b <- calibrate(dclus1, ~stype+api99, c(pop.totals, api99=3914069), bounds=c(0,1.5))) 1 - level Cluster Sampling design With (15) clusters. calibrate(dclus1, ~stype + api99, c(pop.totals, api99 = 3914069), bounds = c(0, 1.5)) > range(weights(dclus1g3b)/weights(dclus1)) [1] 0.4970466 1.5000000. > (dclus1g3b <- calibrate(dclus1, ~stype+api99, c(pop.totals, api99=3914069), bounds=c(0.5,1.5))) Error in calibrate.survey.design2(dclus1, ~stype + api99, c(pop.totals, : Failed to achieve bounds in 11 iterations. > (dclus1agg<-calibrate(dclus1, ~stype, pop.totals, aggregate.stage=1)) 1 - level Cluster Sampling design With (15) clusters. calibrate(dclus1, ~stype, pop.totals, aggregate.stage = 1). > (rclus1agg3 <- calibrate(rclus1, ~stype+api99, c(pop.totals,api99=3914069), aggregate.index=~dnum)) Call: calibrate(rclus1, ~stype + api99, c(pop.totals, api99 = 3914069), aggregate.index = ~dnum) Unstratified cluster jacknife (JK1) with 15 replicates. For example, we can perform logit calibration of the one-stage cluster sample:. > dclus1g3d <- calibrate(dclus1, ~stype + api99, c(pop.totals, + api99 = 3914069), calfun = "logit", bounds = c(0.5, 2.5)) > summary(weights(dclus1g3d)/weights(dclus1)) Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max.

results.title: Post-stratification and calibration | Sampling Surveys Class Notes
results.content: ## 13.2 Post-stratification and calibration. # 13.2 Post-stratification and calibration. 13.2 Post-stratification and calibration. Post-stratification and calibration are powerful tools for improving survey accuracy. They use known population info to adjust estimates, reducing bias from non-response and sampling errors. The choice between post-stratification and calibration depends on the type and quality of available auxiliary data. ## Post-Stratification and Calibration Estimators. * Post-stratification adjusts survey estimates using population information known after data collection. * Improves precision of estimates by reducing sampling variability. ### Calibration and Regression Estimators. * Calibration estimators adjust sample weights to match known population totals for auxiliary variables. * Raking ratio estimation iteratively adjusts weights to match marginal totals for multiple variables. * General regression estimator (GREG) extends calibration to use linear regression models. * GREG incorporates auxiliary information through a regression model of the survey variable. + $\mathbf{X}$ is the vector of known population totals for auxiliary variables. + $\hat{\mathbf{X}}\_{HT}$ is the Horvitz-Thompson estimator of auxiliary variable totals. * Post-stratification works well with categorical auxiliary variables (age groups, regions). * Calibration estimators handle both categorical and continuous auxiliary information. * GREG estimator often provides more precise estimates than post-stratification. * Raking useful for complex surveys with many auxiliary variables and marginal controls. * Choice of method depends on available auxiliary information and survey design complexity. ## Auxiliary Information. ### Types and Sources of Auxiliary Variables. * Auxiliary variables correlate with survey variables of interest or non-response patterns. * Previous survey results or census data provide reliable auxiliary information. * Quality of auxiliary information impacts effectiveness of calibration techniques. * Population totals refer to known aggregate values of auxiliary variables for the entire target population. * Accuracy of population totals crucial for effective calibration and bias reduction. * Misalignment between survey period and auxiliary data can introduce bias. * Calibration constraints ensure sample weights reproduce known population totals for auxiliary variables. + Where $w\_i$ are the calibrated weights, $x\_i$ are auxiliary variable values, and $X$ is the population total. * Diagnostic tools help assess impact of calibration on weight distribution and estimate precision. * Variance estimation for calibrated estimators requires special techniques (e.g., linearization, replication methods).

results.title: Weighting Techniques | SampleWeighting.com
results.content: # Weighting Techniques Comprehensive guide to different statistical weighting methods and when to use them. Do you want to experience our user-friendly tool for yourself? ## Statistical Weighting Techniques Different weighting techniques serve different research needs. Understanding when and how to apply each method ensures optimal results for your specific survey data and research objectives. ## Common Weighting Techniques ### Post-Stratification Weighting Adjusts sample proportions to match known population characteristics after data collection. Works by creating weight classes based on cross-tabulations of demographic variables. #### Best Used When: * • Complete cross-tabulation data available * • Moderate number of weighting variables #### Limitations: * • Requires complete population cross-tabs * • Can create empty cells with sparse data * • Limited to available benchmark data * • May not handle complex interactions ### Raking (Rim Weighting) Iteratively adjusts weights to match multiple marginal distributions simultaneously. Perfect when you have targets for individual variables but not their interactions. #### Best Used When: * • Targets come from different sources #### Limitations: * • May not preserve variable interactions * • Convergence can be slow or unstable ### Propensity Score Weighting Uses statistical models to predict response probability and adjusts for non-response bias. Particularly effective for complex survey designs with multiple bias sources. #### Best Used When: #### Limitations: * • Assumes data missing at random ### Calibration Weighting Ensures weighted sample totals exactly match known population totals for auxiliary variables. Offers fine-grained control over multiple constraints simultaneously. #### Best Used When: #### Limitations: ## Choosing the Right Technique ### Decision Framework The choice depends on your data characteristics, available auxiliary information, and research objectives. #### By Data Availability #### By Complexity Level → Propensity Scoring (complex bias patterns) ### Implementation Success Tips #### Start Simple Begin with post-stratification before moving to complex methods. #### Validate Results Always check weight distributions and compare methods when possible. #### Document Process Record all decisions and rationale for transparency and replication. ## Get your free trial now! With just a few clicks, you'll have access to our wonderful weighting tool. Let us make it easy for you.

results.title: Survey Sample Size Optimization Techniques
results.content: Survey Sample Size Optimization Techniques Survey Sample Size Optimization Techniques Strategies for Refining Survey Samples: Key Adjustments Sarah Lee AI generated o3-mini 10 min read· May 15, 2025 Photo by Edho Pratama on Unsplash * Impact on Effective Sample Size Optimizing survey sample size is critical for achieving accurate and reliable results, especially when surveys are used to inform strategic decisions in business, public policy, and academic research. Our exploration covers the design effect and its mathematical underpinnings, the rationale and mechanics behind data weighting, necessary adjustments when dealing with cluster sampling, and techniques designed to mitigate bias. The design effect quantifies how much the sampling design (often involving clustering, stratification, or unequal probabilities) inflates the variance of an estimate. ### Impact on Effective Sample Size The concept of effective sample size (ESS) helps researchers understand how the design effect diminishes the statistical power of a survey. To capture the relationship visually, consider the following Mermaid diagram that illustrates the concept of effective sample size: This straightforward diagram highlights how the actual number of observations is adjusted according to the design effect. * **Post-Stratification Weights:** After data collection, researchers might adjust the weights so that the survey sample better reflects known population totals, such as age, gender, or education level. ### Adjusting Sample Size When dealing with cluster designs, the effective sample size is adjusted to account for the cluster structure. ### Software Options Several software solutions offer integrated routines for survey sample size optimization, design effect adjustments, weighting, and bias mitigation. The software includes robust commands like svyset and survey estimation commands, streamlining complex data adjustments according to design effects and clustering. Optimizing survey sample size is both an art and a science—requiring detailed knowledge of statistical theory as well as practical experience with data collection challenges. From the fundamentals of the design effect and the calculation of effective sample sizes to advanced weighting adjustments, cluster corrections, and bias mitigation strategies, every element plays a critical role in ensuring that survey results are robust and accurate. Through this article, we have seen how design effect modification can necessitate sample size adjustments, the role of weighting in correcting sample imbalances, the intricacies introduced by clustering, and the multiple strategies available to mitigate bias.

results.title: Design Effects and Effective Sample Size
results.content: Represented as a formula, the design effect is: \[\small deff(\hat{\theta}) = \frac{V\_{complex}(\hat{\theta})}{V\_{SRS}(\hat{\theta})}\] where \(\small \hat{\theta}\) is an estimator of a chosen parameter. The **effective sample size** is the sample size for an estimator \(\small \hat{\theta}\) from a complex sample divided by the design effect of \(\small \hat{\theta}\), i.e. For example, if a complex sample of n=1000 elements has a design effect of 1.25 for some estimate, the effective sample size is \(\small n\_{eff} = 1000/1.25 = 800\). As can be seen, as the homogeneity \(\small \rho\) increases and as cluster sample size \(\small n\_h^{\*}\) increases, the design effect increases. The `survey` package also calculates design effects, using the definitional formula given at the beginning of this vignette, \(\small deff(\hat{\theta}) = \frac{V\_{complex}(\hat{\theta})}{V\_{SRS}(\hat{\theta})}\), by directly estimating the numerator and denominator given the input data. It should be noted that the `survey` package provides only the final summary design effect based on the formula above with no decomposition into components for stratification, clustering, and weighting. Given design effects from previous surveys, the intraclass correlation coefficient \(\small \rho\), which measures the homogeneity within clusters, can be approximated from the formula, \(\small deff\_{clus}\left( {\hat{\theta }} \right) = 1 + \rho \left( \bar{n}-1 \right)\), which comes from the variance for an estimated mean or total. where \(\small deff\_{Clus}(\hat{\theta})\) is the cluster design effect for the estimator \(\small \hat{\theta}\) and \(\small \bar{n}\) is the average number of elements sampled from each cluster. The design effect for different estimates can be very different, even if they are from the same sample and use the same weights. The survey practitioner is advised to calculate design effects on many variables and get a sense of the overall design effects and potential risks to the analytic objectives if the sample size is too small for many, but not all, variables. (See the vignette, “Selection of Appropriate PracTools Sample Size Function” at .) While these sample size formulas can account for design complexities (like stratification and clustering), they do not typically account for the effect of weighting. “A Model Based Justification of Kish’s Formula for Design Effects for Weighting and Clustering.” *Survey Methodology* 25 (1): 105–6.
